nameStory: The snowy tree cricket gets its name from its pale, almost translucent white or cream-colored body that looks frosted like fresh snow. This delicate coloring helps it blend perfectly with light-colored tree bark and pale leaves where it spends most of its time.
description: The snowy tree cricket is a slender, delicate insect about the size of your pinky nail, with a pale greenish-white to cream-colored body. Unlike the chunky black field crickets you might know, tree crickets are graceful and almost translucent, with long, thread-like antennae and broad, clear wings. Males are the musicians of the group, producing the classic chirping sounds we associate with summer evenings by rubbing their wings together.

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Pale greenish-white to cream colored body that appears almost translucent, like looking through frosted glass

idTips.label: Wings
idTips.description: Broad, clear wings that are wider than the body and held flat over the back when at rest

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Extremely long, thin antennae that are much longer than the body and constantly twitch as they explore

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Slender build about half an inch long, much more delicate and narrow than chunky field crickets

idTips.label: Sound
idTips.description: Continuous, musical chirping that sounds like a high-pitched trill rather than individual chirps

habitat: Snowy tree crickets live in trees, shrubs, and tall vegetation throughout New England, preferring deciduous trees like maples, oaks, and fruit trees. You'll find them in orchards, forest edges, parks, and suburban areas with mature trees. They're most common at heights of 3-15 feet off the ground, though you're more likely to hear them than see them.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active. Look for tiny nymphs (young crickets without wings) on new leaves starting in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity begins in mid to late summer when adults emerge and males start their evening concerts. This is the best time to locate them by following their calls.
seasonality.fall: Singing continues into early fall until the first hard frosts. Females lay eggs in tree bark during this time before dying off.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity. Eggs overwinter in tree bark crevices, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: The snowy tree cricket is nature's thermometer! You can calculate the temperature in Fahrenheit by counting the number of chirps in 13 seconds and adding 40 - it's accurate to within a degree or two because their metabolism speeds up in warmer weather.
confusionNotes: Most people confuse tree crickets with field crickets, but remember: tree crickets are pale and delicate like ghosts in the trees, while field crickets are dark and chunky ground-dwellers. If it's singing high up in a tree and looks translucent, it's likely a tree cricket.
contextualKnowledge: You've probably heard snowy tree crickets more than any other insect - their calls are the classic 'summer night' sound effect used in countless movies and TV shows. Hollywood sound engineers love their continuous, romantic trilling over the choppy chirps of other crickets.
compareHints: Among New England's tree crickets, the snowy tree cricket has the palest, most translucent appearance. The narrow-winged tree cricket is similar but slightly more yellowish, while the black-horned tree cricket has distinctive dark markings on its antennae. The snowy's wings are also notably broader than most of its relatives, giving it a more delicate, ethereal appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tree crickets, this species stands out for its narrow wing shape compared to the broad-winged tree cricket's obviously wider wings.

Among New England's tree crickets, Pine Tree Cricket is unique in its exclusive preference for pine trees - Snowy Tree Crickets prefer deciduous trees and shrubs, while Broad-winged Tree Crickets favor fruit trees and berry bushes.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Black-horned is the easiest to identify thanks to its dark antennae.

Among New England's tree crickets, the broad-winged species is distinguished by its wider male wings compared to the narrow-winged tree cricket, and its preference for deciduous trees rather than the pine-loving pine tree cricket.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Four-spotted is the only one with exactly four dark spots on its body.
